#5213. Xsolla ZK’s New Gas Token Aims to Let Digital Items Travel Between Games and Players

Disclaimer: The below article is sponsored, and the views in it do not represent those of ZyCrypto. Readers should conduct independent research before taking any actions related to the project mentioned in this piece. This article should not be regarded as investment advice.

Xsolla ZK, Inc. is introducing Xsolla Gas (XLA), the native token of Xsolla ZK — a blockchain network built for games. XLA is designed to pay the network fees that arise when players transfer or share eligible digital items on Xsolla ZK.

For players who’d rather not download and set up a separate wallet, Xsolla Gas Station, offered by Xsolla (USA), Inc., can cover those fees. There, players buy XLA-NT, a non-transferable gas credit used only to pay network fees on Xsolla ZK. (Xsolla Gas Station sells only XLA-NT.)

Players want more from the games and brands they follow, and developers want new ways to engage them. Digital items have evolved well beyond cosmetics — players now collect them from their favorite games. But letting players keep, share, and give away those items has long been complicated.

Most digital items today live on a single game’s backend. Players generally can’t transfer them to friends or carry them into another game, and the items simply vanish if a game shuts down. Blockchain-backed items stay with the players who collect them — but transferring them requires a network fee, which traditionally means setting up and managing a separate digital wallet and acquiring the right token to pay. That friction adds up.

Xsolla ZK is designed to remove that friction. Xsolla’s existing payment, monetization, and distribution products can now support blockchain-backed items — giving developers a new way to monetize and distribute digital items, and giving players new ways to keep them and pass them on.

Players use Xsolla Gas to cover the network fees required to transfer or share a digital item held in their Xsolla Backpack.

Xsolla Backpack is an inventory for the digital items a player owns. Items issued to the Backpack in transferable form are designed to remain available to the player even if the issuing game shuts down — and can be given to another player.

The intent is to put players in control of what happens to the eligible items they own. Digital items that remain on a game’s own backend continue to work exactly as they do today and can’t be transferred through Backpack.

Players who want to collect these items simply sign in to their account as usual — no seed phrase, no separate wallet setup. They cover network fees by buying XLA-NT gas credits through Xsolla Gas Station, using the payment methods they already know and prefer.

From there, players can collect eligible items they purchase or claim in their Backpack and share them with other players.

“Players should be able to share and gift digital items they own, anytime, anywhere, with anyone they know,” said Chris Hewish, President of Xsolla (USA). “Developers gain a new way to monetize their games, and players gain eligible digital items that are theirs to keep. When both sides win, the games do too. We are adding options inside the tools they already use, not asking anyone to change how they work.”

When a player wants to share or give away a digital item, the transaction runs on Xsolla ZK, the blockchain network, and the network fee is paid in Xsolla Gas. This lets players hold items and pass them on to others, and it’s designed to let them carry items between supported games.

Players can cover the fee themselves in XLA or XLA-NT, while developers and partners can use XLA to pay network fees for their own item activity.

More than 1,500 game teams use Xsolla (USA)’s tools and services to monetize and distribute games. Those tools are designed to work with Xsolla ZK to support the transfer of eligible digital items — and Xsolla Backpack and Xsolla Gas Station are now available without additional development for teams using compatible Xsolla (USA) products, integrating directly with existing player and payment flows.

Studios, publishers, brands, and players can learn more about Xsolla Gas Station at x.la/gas. Developers building games, wallets, marketplaces, and item services on Xsolla ZK can find network documentation, developer tools, and integration paths at xsolla.org.

Readers can also complete a short Xsolla Quest at xsolla.pro/xsolla-zk-quest to learn more about Xsolla Gas, Xsolla Gas Station, and Xsolla Backpack.

What is Xsolla Quest? Xsolla Quest lets people complete a few simple steps on an Xsolla page to receive an item.

#5212. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

#5210. Revolut’s Italian Business Faces Court Oversight: 265 Warnings, Zero Suspicious Reports

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

A Milan court has put Revolut’s Italian branch under judicial administration for one year, in a ruling dated November 12 that came to light on Monday. The Revolut investigation found that the bank’s anti-money laundering checks let suspected criminals move money through it for five years.

Italy: A Milan court has placed the Italian operations of digital banking giant Revolut under judicial administration for one year after investigators uncovered serious anti-money-laundering failures involving mafia-linked suspects and convicted criminals.Prosecutors identified… pic.twitter.com/8b5WkfDdad

The court found that at least 24 clients moved or hid about €41.9 million through Revolut accounts between 2021 and 2026. All of them are under investigation or already convicted, and some have suspected mafia ties. Two court-appointed administrators will now work alongside the bank’s managers on customer checks and transaction monitoring.

We lined up the figures from the ruling. Other banks filed 265 suspicious-transaction reports on those same 24 people, about 11 each. Revolut filed none.

Revolut is not under criminal investigation, and it says its services in Italy, where it has more than 5 million customers, will keep running normally. The case also reaches into crypto. It began with a 2024 police inspection of Revolut Digital Assets Europe, the unit that serves the app’s crypto users in Europe.

The order targets Revolut Bank UAB, the Lithuanian-licensed bank that runs the Italian branch. Milan prosecutor Paolo Storari asked for it after the Revolut investigation by the Guardia di Finanza, Italy’s financial police.

Judicial administration is a preventive measure, not a penalty. Italian courts have used it on fashion and logistics companies to fix weak controls without taking over the business. In the 39-page ruling, the court said Revolut’s failures were “embedded in a stable management model, repeatedly applied over time.” Prosecutors called the bank a “financial reservoir” for serious criminals.

Revolut said it takes its “regulatory obligations and anti-money laundering controls extremely seriously” and will cooperate fully.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

The ruling’s sharpest number is the gap in suspicious-transaction reports, the alerts banks must send to Italy’s financial intelligence unit (UIF) when money looks dirty. Rival banks flagged the same 24 people 265 times. Revolut, which held their accounts too, sent nothing. That gap sits at the center of the Revolut investigation.

The suspects are linked to money laundering, tax fraud, extortion, and drug cases, some with suspected mafia ties. Prosecutors say there is no evidence that Revolut knowingly took part in their schemes. The case is about controls that didn’t catch them.

The Revolut investigation started with crypto. In 2024, Milan’s financial police inspected Revolut Digital Assets Europe, formerly RT Digital Securities Cyprus. That is the company that runs crypto trading for the app’s users across Europe, under a MiCA licence from Cyprus.

The police report, finished in December 2024, alleged more than 1 million breaches of customer due diligence and record-keeping rules and 60 failures to report suspicious transactions. It went to Italy’s Economy Ministry, which can fine the company. The ministry hasn’t opened sanction proceedings yet, and Revolut’s window to object runs into 2027.

Two more reviews are under way. The UIF has finished its own inspection of the Italian branch and is due to report soon. Bank of Italy inspectors are also checking how the bank handles transparency and customer-protection rules.

The Milan order adds to a run of trouble in Europe. Lithuania’s central bank fined Revolut Bank €3.5 million in April 2025 over gaps in how it monitored transactions, its largest fine at the time. In April 2026, Italy’s competition authority fined Revolut over €11 million for unfair practices, including blocking payment accounts without warning. Revolut said it would appeal.

The timing matters beyond Italy. Revolut has conditional approval for a US national bank charter. Cetin Duransoy, head of its US unit, said on Monday that “a massive hiccup somewhere” can have an impact in other places.

Counting from the November 12 ruling, the dates to watch are:

For Revolut’s customers in Italy, nothing changes today. Accounts, cards and crypto trading keep working, and the administrators don’t touch customer money. The risk is to the bank’s growth: stricter checks can mean more questions at sign-up and more frozen transfers, the same practice Italy’s watchdog fined it for in April.

According to CoinGlass, the cumulative volume delta (CVD) on the Coinbase spot market reached -$1.08 billion between Oct. 31 and Nov. 15. CVD shows the difference between the volume of market buy orders and market sell orders, and a negative CVD means that sellers were more active on the exchange.

Over the same period, the CVD on the spot markets of OKX, Bybit and Binance stood at $240.3 million, $65.17 million and $51.88 million, respectively, so buyers were more active on these three exchanges.

The price of Bitcoin went down from $81,188 on Nov. 4 to $61,956 on Nov. 14, according to CoinGlass data, and the decline amounted to around 24%. On Sunday, Bitcoin recovered to around $65,400.

The data comes amid claims that Binance has been pushing the price of Bitcoin down. The exchange lost $6.4 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, and some users on X then claimed that Binance was selling crypto to cover its losses. Two weeks after the attack, Binance published a Proof of Reserves report that showed client balances on the exchange were fully backed.

This week, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared a comparison of Bitcoin charts ahead of the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs and called it "an interesting analysis." Several users in the replies to his post blamed the drop in Bitcoin on selling by Binance.

Binance is the largest crypto exchange by trading volume, and a large share of futures liquidations takes place on the platform. On Nov. 13, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion in 24 hours, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Still, the CVD on the Binance spot market has stayed positive since Oct. 31.

Coinbase is the custodian for most U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, including BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, and many U.S. institutional investors trade on the platform through Coinbase Prime.

Anthropic is set to start trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19, and the selling on Coinbase comes ahead of the listing. Fundstrat managing partner Tom Lee has called the recent drawdown in Bitcoin a temporary rotation of money into mega-IPOs, and in the 50 days before the Anthropic IPO, Bitcoin has lost around 18%.

#5205. Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Coinbase is bringing crypto trading directly into ChatGPT as competition for AI-powered financial services intensifies. Meanwhile, PancakeSwap has dropped “Swap” from its name, expanding beyond decentralized trading. The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration last night, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

Trade Base assets from ChatGPT@ChatGPT now connects to your Coinbase account, so you can trade Base assets in chat pic.twitter.com/tg9r2Iv3Qe

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible users to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. Users must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single…

The integration also builds on Coinbase’s AI infrastructure. Its Coinbase for Agents toolkit provides developers with connections to trading accounts and market data. The ChatGPT launch brings those capabilities into a more accessible consumer interface.

As of today, the official integration currently remains limited to eligible U.S. Coinbase users. It also depends on ChatGPT account and workspace availability.

new brand, who dis?PancakeSwap is now Pancake 🥞6 years ago we were known for one thing. Today, we’re More Than a Swap. Let us reintroduce ourselves 👇 pic.twitter.com/J3P7Mocu2P

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform announced its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million users and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

Its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

These agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

#5202. XRP Ledger Passes 11.7 Million Sub-Dollar AI Agent Microtransactions

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Chandler Fang, founder of AI payments startup t54.ai, has said that the company's x402 Facilitator on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has processed more than 10 million AI agent transactions. Fang made the comments in an interview that the XRPL Foundation published on X on November 15, and the interviewer put the number of these payments at 11.7 million.

According to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very quickly in the three months," he said.

The x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang said that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

According to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang said.

Fang said that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower users to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

According to Fang, trust is the main issue for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang said.

t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang said that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

"The ten million transactions are just a starting point. I think next year you should expect a lot more transactions. Maybe even more transactions settled on XRPL will be done by AI agents than by humans," Fang said.

#5201. Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path shows how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem shows pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

#5200. Binance Warns About AI Scams

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.

The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its users that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.

"AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange said in a post.

The cryptocurrency exchange has assured its users that no one from Binance will ever reach out to them asking for money or offering unsolicited investment advice.

Binance says scammers are making realistic deepfake videos featuring executives and employees of the company.

Fraudsters are using these deepfakes, some of which are very realistic, to trick potential targets through fraudulent video calls.

That way, people who fall victim to the scam might think they are interacting with real Binance personnel.

Binance warned that scammers often try to reach potential targets through messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram. They impersonate Binance employees by using their names, photos, and job titles to appear credible.

After making contact with a potential victim, the scammer may try to convince them to send crypto, take part in an exclusive investment opportunity, or take other financial actions.

Binance has called on crypto users to be cautious about any unexpected messages they receive, even if they seem to be from someone at the company they know.

A realistic appearance no longer guarantees a person's identity, given that AI can now easily mimic voices and facial expressions.

Users should double-check any suspicious messages through official Binance support channels before taking any action.

Shiba Inu has been struggling on the market for ages, and November 14 made things worse: SHIB broke below its July low of $0.00000413 and dipped to around $0.0000037.

SHIB mostly followed the uptrend from July to October, but tumbled quickly due to the general reversal of the cryptocurrency market. The bounce from the July level was unlikely to occur naturally, and the zone where some buy orders might have been concentrated didn't hold.

Back in September, the 200 EMA acted as strong resistance that SHIB was unable to break, and the asset has been sliding ever since. The ascending trendline from July was lost back in October.

SHIB is trading at $0.00000391, bouncing slightly from the low. The drop below $0.000004 isn't a guarantee of anything, as SHIB has already been lower in previous years. RSI is moving around 25, deep in the oversold zone. Multiple indicators suggest a retrace, but the overall market picture is grim, to say the least.

According to CryptoQuant, SHIB held on exchanges is worth around $332 million, while the netflow stays negative. In tokens, around 86 trillion SHIB still sit on exchanges. Most of the activity is still most likely fueled by retail investors, as the largest players stay sidelined or are not exposed to SHIB at all.

Shiba Inu volumes are still low, which suggests a lack of volatility ahead. The market is weak, and it might get weaker, though most of the selling pressure SHIB could face has most likely been injected already.

The death cross we are witnessing on the EMAs is important, but barely significant for the asset itself. It is a mere reflection of market sentiment, rather than anything else. The short-term moving average is falling rapidly, which suggests an extremely negative short-term dynamic.

The blue moving average crossed below the black one at around $96, roughly 25% above the current price. Realistically, the closest "fair" support is the $60 price level, where Solana bounced back in June.

A better time to buy Solana could be tied to an overall market recovery, which needs a stronger market catalyst that does not exist at this point. Unfortunately, there are little to no fundamental factors that can help Solana reach key market levels right now.

Zcash rapidly dived toward the 200 EMA, and the downtrend isn't going anywhere. However, the situation is very different from Solana. A solid support still exists for the price, and the situation is not as dire.

ZEC is trading at $915, up almost 6% today after a wick toward $800 on November 14. The longest moving average is still moving below the price, suggesting the long-term uptrend isn't broken yet.

The NU7 update, activated on November 6, also made the Zcash network somewhat healthier by decreasing the target block interval to 25 seconds.

The price violated the $1,000 level, and the moving averages are trying to converge rapidly. The convergence of moving averages might lead to a volatility spike. From the momentum perspective, RSI is close to 30, so the asset is almost oversold.

In order to avoid a deeper correction, Zcash must reclaim the $1,000 price level. If the price violates the 200 EMA, our next stop would be the $800 area, which acts as a psychological threshold rather than a strong technical level.

#5197. Tokenized Stocks Open 24/7 on OKXICE, but Only Crypto Firms Signed Up: Will Wall Street Follow?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. OKXICE, the joint venture of crypto exchange OKX and NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), opens round-the-clock trading in tokenized stocks for eligible US customers on Sunday, November 23. The only companies whose shares it will offer at launch are crypto firms: Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize.

Of the 62 companies the venue first picked, 56 objected. Its November 5 notice lists 67 objectors in all, including every member of the Magnificent Seven.

⚡️JUST IN: OKX and NYSE parent ICE will launch 24/7 tokenized U.S. securities trading on November 23 through their joint venture, OKXICE.More than 70 assets are expected, including Coinbase, Circle, Robinhood, and Strategy securities, plus 59 Direxion ETFs.The platform will… pic.twitter.com/TfRuuZrcV0

That leaves buyers with a narrow menu. We checked what they will actually get: the six stocks are down a median 42% this year, while the S&P 500 is up 7%. Five of the six have moved more closely with Bitcoin than the S&P 500 has over the past three months.

The launch is the first real test of a new SEC rule meant to bring listed shares onto blockchains. So will Wall Street follow, or is this a crypto-only market for now?

Explore: Will Tokenized Stocks Move by xStocks Bring New Volume to HSBC, Shell and Other European Equities?

A tokenized stock is a blockchain token that tracks a listed share. ICE set up the venture after it invested in OKX in March at a $25 billion valuation. On OKXICE, each token is backed by a real US share, and customers hold it in a self-custody wallet inside the OKX app.

The venue runs under an exemption the SEC issued on September 17. It lets blockchain venues trade tokenized versions of listed US shares without registering as an exchange, for up to five years. Companies are not asked to opt in. Instead, each one gets 30 days after being notified to object, and silence counts as consent.

Most said no. Applied Optoelectronics said it was worried about pricing, liquidity and volatility, and that investors might think it backed the product. The OKXICE launch page confirms the November 23 start, with more than 70 assets, 59 of them exchange-traded funds from Direxion.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

We pulled daily prices for the six launch stocks from Yahoo Finance. Then we measured how far each has moved in 2026 and how closely its daily moves tracked Bitcoin over the past 90 trading days.

So a US investor who wanted Apple or Nvidia around the clock gets, for now, five stocks that rise and fall with the crypto market. ICE’s own shares, by comparison, are up 8% this year and barely track Bitcoin at all, with a correlation of 0.08.

The objections don’t mean Wall Street is ignoring tokenization. It is building its own version first.

In March, the SEC approved a Nasdaq pilot that puts tokenized and regular shares in the same order book. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), which settles most US stock trades, runs a tokenization service with 20 participants and 34 securities. In September, Nasdaq agreed to invest $100 million in Payward, the parent of crypto exchange Kraken, to build infrastructure for tokenized shares.

The difference is control. In those projects, exchanges and clearing houses run the system, and trading stays tied to regular market hours and rules. OKXICE offers 24/7 trading, which companies have pushed back on: a share that trades all weekend leaves no quiet time to handle bad news. Nasdaq has also warned that splitting trading across separate venues could thin out liquidity.

So the answer is “not yet.” Wall Street is likely to reach tokenized stocks through its own exchanges and DTCC before it lets crypto venues list its shares.

Robinhood is the launch name with the most at stake: it already sells tokenized stocks to European customers. Its 24/7 contract on Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange that lists perpetual futures on US stocks, trades at $70.32.

On the daily chart, HOOD sits far below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $90.17, and its 200-day EMA at $97.99.

XYZ:HOODUSD 1D chart. Source: Hyperliquid

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

The number to watch after Sunday is not OKXICE’s volume but its objection list. The first large non-crypto company to stay off it would be the clearest sign that Wall Street is ready to follow tokenized stocks onto a crypto venue.

#5196. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

#5195. Brazil Takes Aim at Stablecoins With Shocking Money Laundering Claim

The head of the foreign exchange department at the Central Bank of Brazil has claimed that legitimately obtained money could be considered laundered if it’s used to purchase stablecoins.

The senior Brazilian official claimed that converting money into stablecoins could link it to money laundering, even when it was initially obtained legally.

According to a recent report, Gerson Romantini, who is the director of the foreign exchange department at the Central Bank of Brazil, allegedly made the controversial statements at a private event attended by representatives of financial companies.

Romantini claimed that funds acquired legally could be transformed once they enter the stablecoin ecosystem.

In his view, even legally obtained money could effectively be "dirtied" if used in certain stablecoin schemes, and thus be considered part of a money laundering operation.

It’s important to note that the comments attributed to Romantini do not represent an official statement that all conversions into stablecoins could be considered money laundering.

This statement comes as Brazil has already moved to tighten restrictions on how cryptocurrencies are used for international payments.

On April 30, the Central Bank of Brazil published Resolution No. 561, which took effect on Oct. 1.

The resolution limits the use of virtual assets for the settlement of international payment and transfer services, also known as eFX.

In practice, this means that payments between an eFX provider and its foreign partner must be settled through traditional foreign exchange operations or a Brazilian real account opened by nonresidents.

Crypto payments for these particular settlements are off-limits.

A practice called the "stablecoin sandwich" is particularly concerning.

The way it works is that a Brazilian fintech accepts a certain amount of reais from a customer, then uses this money to purchase stablecoins like USDT or USDC and sends the funds in crypto to an offshore company.

This company, in turn, can convert these stablecoins into fiat currency to make payments or send money to families.

This allows users to make international money transfers for a lower fee and circumvent some of the infrastructure banks use.

The controversial statements have already received a response from Brazil’s crypto industry.

In a statement on Nov. 14, the Brazilian Association of Tokenization and Digital Assets (ABToken) questioned the alleged classification of stablecoin transactions as money laundering.

ABToken maintains that the use of stablecoins is not necessarily illegal.

Furthermore, the association also cautioned that sweeping bans may create legal confusion and hinder legitimate business activities that use stablecoins for international payments.

#5194. Vitalik Buterin Breaks Silence on New Ethereum (ETH) Update

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has published a lengthy post on EIP-8037, a change planned for the Glamsterdam upgrade. In his latest post, Buterin wrote that something like EIP-8037 is, unfortunately, the only way for Ethereum to scale safely.

With the update, Ethereum will collect an additional gas fee for the creation of new accounts. Creating a new account would cost more than five times as much gas as it does now, with new storage slots and contracts getting more expensive too.

According to Buterin, execution is easy to scale, but Ethereum's state already grows by around 110 GiB per year, and every node has to keep it.

Unfortunately, it will bring more pressure on existing contracts, for example, the OP Stack bridge. The bridge has a hardcoded gas limit of 40,000, and even a small increase in state gas costs would push its operation above it. Mainnet has at least 13 contracts like that, according to the security firm ChainSecurity.

It's a double-edged sword: from one standpoint, it limits the ability of spammers and scammers to fill the network with junk accounts used by illicit actors; from the other, it creates additional financial pressure.

Glamsterdam being postponed is another pain factor here: considering the poor state of the market and Ethereum's struggle, it's clear that any delays in major updates negatively affect the network outlook. The new date is yet to be confirmed.

Vitalik Buterin has been hinting at the change in gas consumption for ages now. Back in 2024, he called multidimensional gas the hardest problem in his own post on the topic.

Setting strict limits was never a farsighted option, and developers have been told that for years. However, it's yet another question: who's actually to blame? Buterin himself admitted that this rule hasn't been written down or repeated since 2021, so newer developers simply didn't know about it.

He now suggests writing down a list of features that are likely to change, from gas mechanics to slot time.

#5193. Major Wealth Advisor With $24 Billion in Assets Discloses XRP ETF Stake

Major U.S. wealth management company EP Wealth Advisors has revealed that it holds an investment in an XRP exchange-traded fund (ETF). This was disclosed in the company's latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

EP Wealth Advisors, a California-based investment advisory firm with about $24.4 billion in securities holdings, has revealed that it held 18,400 shares in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This was disclosed in the official SEC filing that the company submitted to the commission on Nov. 13. The filing showed that the investment was valued at $147,936 at the end of the third quarter.

Furthermore, the filing showed that the total portfolio value reported by EP Wealth Advisors stood at $24,380,879,896. This value comprises 1,603 items in the company's 13F information table.

It's worth noting, however, that this isn't the company's total assets under management. It's the value of its reportable securities holdings. There are also assets that are not included in Form 13F.

Interestingly, this isn't the first time EP Wealth Advisors has held an investment in XRPI. Data from its historical 13F filings shows that in the second quarter of 2026, the wealth management company held 13,425 shares in XRPI.

The recent filing shows that the company has now increased the number of shares it holds in the XRP ETF by 4,975 shares. This represents about a 37% increase in the company's XRPI holdings during the third quarter.

Nevertheless, this amount is very small relative to the company's multibillion-dollar securities portfolio. It represents less than 0.01% of the total value of its reported securities holdings.

It's also worth reiterating that Form 13F is simply a filing that shows institutional holdings at the end of a quarter. It doesn't necessarily represent the investment manager's current holdings.

The Volatility Shares XRP ETF was launched in May 2025. Its ticker symbol is XRPI, and it is currently trading on Nasdaq.

XRPI isn't a spot XRP ETF. This means it doesn't directly hold the cryptocurrency XRP. Rather, it primarily derives its exposure to XRP's price movements through XRP futures contracts.

This ETF essentially provides investors with a way to invest in XRP without actually having to hold or custody the cryptocurrency. The ETF aims to deliver investment returns that correlate with the performance of XRP.

As of Nov. 13, the most recent available data from the fund issuer shows that XRPI's net assets stood at about $77.9 million.

#5192. Etherscan Hacked? Crypto Users Have Had Enough as Support Security Scare Sparks Alarm

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting unauthorized access attempts against its customer support system that might have been hacked. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Etherscan disclosed just a few minutes ago that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In…

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal crypto and your money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Yet, it has greater effects to geopolitics.

Germany’s BIGGEST bank just had its secrets leaked.15 MILLION files. Epstein. Trump. Russia. Colombia. Nearly $600 MILLION in suspicious payments.And almost NOBODY is talking about it…Deutsche Bank says the matters “date back many years and in some cases as much as two…

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan possibly being hacked, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies investigating security incidents.

#5191. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has replied to XRP holders who criticized him for selling most of his XRP with a Saturday Night Live GIF of Natalie Portman saying, "I never said I was a role model."

According to Schwartz, his XRP holdings are down 88%, from a peak of roughly 26 million tokens to 3 million. His Bitcoin went from about 1,500 coins to one, and his Ether went from about 40,000 to six.

Schwartz wrote that he "really doesn't like risk." According to Schwartz, he and his wife agreed years ago to sell some of their coins every time crypto reached a new all-time high. In 2025, Schwartz sold around 2.5 million XRP and paid about $1.7 million in capital gains tax on the sale. He had received these tokens in 2020 and 2023.

@hllywd22 @tchdwntommyd @WHTBOYRICKY @CryptoTaxFixer When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous. What BTC hit $200, that seemed ridiculous.

Schwartz said that all of his sales were made under written trading plans, and a lawyer approved each plan at least 30 days before each sale. According to Schwartz, his largest risk asset is still his stake in Ripple.

Schwartz also said that he was a skeptic from the start and did not believe in the early price records of crypto. "When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous," he wrote.

In his view, the price of XRP today depends on overall sentiment in the crypto market, and fees on the network barely move it. Schwartz allows that the token could capture some of the value of a successful ecosystem in the future, but there are no guarantees. On Monday, the price of XRP stands at $0.956.

On Nov. 16, Schwartz also posted a review of the XRPL codebase by the Qwen AI model. "I asked Qwen to rate my work on the XRPL software. It was mostly good. But this was harsh and it's not wrong," he wrote.

According to the review, the overall architecture of XRPL is good. Still, Qwen said that some components of the code are too tightly coupled, and the migration to a new testing framework stopped halfway. The AI model also called the code generation in XRPL opaque.

Several XRPL developers replied to the post and said that they are already rewriting some of these parts of the code. Other users asked for formal verification of the XRPL core before the new features planned for 2027 go live.

Publicly listed Bitcoin miners have sold nearly half of their Bitcoin since January. Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode published the report today, November 18. The miners are using the coins to pay for a move into AI data centers. Its chart of six miners, led by MARA Holdings, shows combined holdings falling from about 110,000 BTC early this year, with the biggest monthly drop coming in November.

Bitcoin miners are rapidly selling their reserves.For years, listed miners held what they mined, and some bought more. Since January, they have sold nearly half their bitcoin:native.A major shift in their approach: the BTC now funds their move into AI data centers. pic.twitter.com/Pe3bE0YJ19

For years, these companies held what they mined, and some bought more. That made them steady holders in the Bitcoin market. Now they are sellers, at a time when the price is already down 28% this year.

We used these data to check whether the switch helped shareholders of these Bitcoin miners. Four of the six stocks fell more than Bitcoin this year, with a median loss of 41%. Only Riot Platforms and Hut 8 are up.

So who is selling, and what does it mean for the Bitcoin price?

Discover: Tokenized Stocks Open 24/7 on OKXICE, but Only Crypto Firms Signed Up: Will Wall Street Follow?

Glassnode tracks the Bitcoin that six listed miners report holding: MARA Holdings, Riot Platforms, CleanSpark, Hut 8, American Bitcoin and Cango. From 2021 to late 2025, their combined stack only grew. This year, it has shrunk in most months, and November’s drop is the largest on the chart.

MARA, the largest holder, accounts for most of it. Its latest filing shows it sold 13,597 BTC for about $1.1 billion over six weeks, at an average price of about $81,000. It used $750 million to repay a loan backed by its Bitcoin and said it would keep selling to build cash for AI infrastructure.

The reason is money. Since the April 2024 halving, each block pays half as much Bitcoin, and the price has fallen from its peak. Renting power and buildings to AI companies pays steadier income, and the coins on the balance sheet are the fastest way to fund the switch.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

We compared each company’s share price this year with Bitcoin’s 28% drop, using Yahoo Finance daily closes from January 2 to November 17.

MARA’s timing looks better than its stock. It sold at about $81,000 on average, roughly 27% above Bitcoin’s $63,947 today.

Sales by Bitcoin miners add supply, but MARA’s $1.1 billion over six weeks is small next to a market worth about $1.3 trillion. The bigger change is in behavior: a group that used to soak up coins now sells them.

That matters most when demand is weak, as it is now. The Fear & Greed Index, a daily sentiment gauge from 0 to 100, sits at 11, in “extreme fear.” Each miner sale adds to the coins buyers have to absorb.

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $63,947. Its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, has just slipped below its 200-day EMA, at about $75,750 each. Traders call that a “death cross,” a sign that the longer downtrend is taking over.

Bitcoin miners won’t go back to hoarding soon. The AI build-out needs cash for years, and their coins are the cheapest source of it. The next sign to watch is December’s holdings data, which will show whether November was a one-off or the new normal.

Since early November, XRP has lost roughly 30% of its value and given up everything it built throughout the August rally. In October, the 200 EMA acted as a strong resistance that XRP was unable to break.

The main problem here is the lack of bullish narratives on the market. Bitcoin lost almost 15% of its value in the blink of an eye, without any solid catalysts or news, apart from ones that have been around for months now: AI, the Nvidia crash, the Anthropic IPO and cybersecurity risks. On November 15, BTC touched a four-month low around $62,000.

Investors aren't buying XRP en masse either. US-listed XRP ETFs saw $19.13 million in net outflows in the week through November 13, the heaviest weekly redemption since March.

The possibility of a recovery is real, but it is minuscule. The RSI dipped below 25 before the bounce, so part of yesterday's move is simply a reaction to the oversold market. There are little to no fundamental factors that can help XRP stay above key levels for longer than a day or two.

Whether buyers can reclaim the $1 level or not is the main test for XRP this week. A short-lived price bounce here won't change the situation as a whole, unfortunately.
